steps.observation: Work on this for 30 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here’s a concise but thorough comparison of the two nucleic acids you encounter most in biology.

1. Chemical makeup  
   • Sugar  
     – DNA: deoxyribose (lacks an –OH group on the 2′ carbon)  
     – RNA: ribose (has an –OH group on the 2′ carbon)  
   • Nitrogenous bases  
     – DNA: adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), thymine (T)  
     – RNA: adenine, guanine, cytosine, uracil (U) instead of thymine  
   • Strand length & shape  
     – DNA: usually long, double-stranded, antiparallel helix (B-form predominates)  
     – RNA: usually shorter, single-stranded, but can fold into complex 3-D shapes with intramolecular base-pairing

2. Stability  
   • The missing 2′-OH in DNA makes its backbone less prone to hydrolysis, so DNA is chemically more stable—ideal for long-term information storage.  
   • RNA’s extra 2′-OH renders it more reactive and susceptible to alkaline degradation, which is useful for molecules meant to be temporary.

3. Functions  
   • DNA: primary, uniform role—long-term storage of hereditary information; template for its own replication and for RNA synthesis (transcription).  
   • RNA: multiple, specialized roles. Major categories include  
     – mRNA (messenger) – carries coding sequences to ribosomes  
     – rRNA (ribosomal) – catalytic and structural core of ribosomes  
     – tRNA (transfer) – brings amino acids during translation  
     – snRNA, snoRNA, miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA, CRISPR RNA, etc.—diverse regulatory or catalytic tasks

4. Cellular location  
   • Eukaryotes: DNA is mostly confined to the nucleus (plus mitochondria/chloroplasts); RNA is synthesized in the nucleus then functions mainly in the cytoplasm (or specific organelles).  
   • Prokaryotes: both DNA and RNA share the same cytoplasmic space, separated only in time during transcription/translation.

5. Replication vs. transcription/translation  
   • DNA replicates semi-conservatively before cell division.  
   • RNA is transcribed continually as needed; most RNAs are not replicated (except in some RNA viruses).

6. Proofreading and mutation rates  
   • DNA polymerases have proofreading ability and, along with repair pathways, keep mutation rates low.  
   • RNA polymerases lack extensive proofreading, leading to a higher error rate—acceptable because many RNA molecules are short-lived.

7. Biological rationale  
   • DNA’s stability suits it to be a durable archive protected in chromosomes.  
   • RNA’s versatility and reactivity allow it to act as both information carrier and catalyst, echoing its theorized role in the RNA world before modern DNA/protein life evolved.
